hints: Express $z$ in Cartesian form so that its real and imaginary parts can be related to the given argument.
Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate $3-ai$ and simplify using $i^2=-1$.
Because $\arg z=-\pi/4$, the point lies in the fourth quadrant with imaginary part equal to the negative of its real part; form the resulting equation in $a$.
Solve it and use the condition that $a$ is an integer, then substitute the admissible value back into the original expression for $z$.
walkthrough:
Multiply numerator and denominator of $z = \dfrac{5a - 2\mathrm{i}}{3 + a\mathrm{i}}$ by the conjugate $(3 - a\mathrm{i})$:
$$z = \dfrac{(5a - 2\mathrm{i})(3 - a\mathrm{i})}{(3 + a\mathrm{i})(3 - a\mathrm{i})} = \dfrac{15a - 5a^2\mathrm{i} - 6\mathrm{i} + 2a\mathrm{i}^2}{3^2 - (a\mathrm{i})^2}$$

Simplify the real and imaginary parts using $\mathrm{i}^2 = -1$:
$$z = \dfrac{15a - 2a - (5a^2 + 6)\mathrm{i}}{9 + a^2} = \dfrac{13a - (5a^2 + 6)\mathrm{i}}{9 + a^2}$$

Separate into Cartesian components:
$$\operatorname{Re}(z) = \dfrac{13a}{9 + a^2}, \quad \operatorname{Im}(z) = -\dfrac{5a^2 + 6}{9 + a^2}$$

Use the given condition $\arg z = -\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
In the fourth quadrant with argument $-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, the real and imaginary parts satisfy $\tan\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = -1$:
$$\dfrac{\operatorname{Im}(z)}{\operatorname{Re}(z)} = \dfrac{-(5a^2 + 6)}{13a} = -1$$
$$\dfrac{5a^2 + 6}{13a} = 1$$

Form and solve the quadratic equation in $a$:
$$5a^2 - 13a + 6 = 0$$
$$(5a - 3)(a - 2) = 0$$
$$a = \dfrac{3}{5} \quad \text{or} \quad a = 2$$

Apply the condition that $a$ is an integer to select $a = 2$, and find $z$:
$$\operatorname{Re}(z) = \dfrac{13(2)}{9 + 2^2} = \dfrac{26}{13} = 2$$
$$\operatorname{Im}(z) = -\dfrac{5(2^2) + 6}{9 + 2^2} = -\dfrac{26}{13} = -2$$
$$z = 2 - 2\mathrm{i}$$

hints: Use the Cartesian value of $z$ from part (a) to find its modulus and argument, then apply the power rule in polar form.
For $z=2-2i$, calculate $|z|$ exactly and use the already stated argument $-\pi/4$.
For $z^3$, cube the modulus and multiply the argument by $3$.
Check that the resulting argument lies in $-\pi<\theta\leq\pi$, then write the result as $re^{i\theta}$ with $r>0$.
walkthrough:
Calculate the modulus $r$ of $z^3$ using the modulus property $|z^3| = |z|^3$:
$$r = (2\sqrt{2})^3 = 2^3 \times (\sqrt{2})^3 = 8 \times 2\sqrt{2} = 16\sqrt{2}$$

Calculate the argument $\theta$ of $z^3$ using the argument property $\arg(z^3) = 3\arg z$:
$$\theta = 3\left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\pi\right) = -\dfrac{3}{4}\pi$$
